blocks.text: The account of Samaria’s fall in verses 9–12 stands beside Sennacherib’s later campaign in Judah in verses 13–16. These are distinct historical horizons: Samaria’s fall is placed in 722/721 BCE, while the Judah campaign is placed in 701 BCE.

The chapter’s notice of siege, deportation, tribute, and invasion should not be compressed into one simple imperial procedure. Assyrian royal claims and the biblical account describe overlapping events, but tribute could arise from different circumstances, and royal records make claims rather than offering a neutral account of an entire campaign.

Lachish is where Hezekiah sends his submission to Sennacherib and from where the Assyrian delegation is dispatched to Jerusalem. A palace relief cycle from Nineveh depicts Lachish’s capture, including captives, booty, and Sennacherib enthroned before the city. It confirms Lachish as a major Assyrian victory in this campaign setting, while its focus on Lachish—not Jerusalem—matters when reading the threat against Jerusalem.

A six-sided clay prism containing Sennacherib’s royal annals independently names Sennacherib, Hezekiah, Judah, tribute, fortified cities, and Jerusalem in the crisis behind this chapter. The overlap helps locate the episode in a wider historical setting, but the annals’ victory-focused rhetoric and sequence differ from Kings, so neither account should simply be treated as a neutral transcript of the other.

The prism names Hezekiah and tribute after the campaign but does not claim Jerusalem’s capture. In the continuation of Kings, Jerusalem is not captured and the Assyrian army withdraws. The comparison establishes historical overlap while preserving differences of perspective, sequence, and interpretation.
